paragraphs: Consumer prices rose 2.6% in September from a year earlier, the slowest annual pace in 18 months, according to Sample Wire's reading of figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. The increase was smaller than economists had forecast, and it was driven in large part by softer housing and vehicle costs.

Rents, the largest single component of the index, climbed at their slowest monthly rate in more than two years. Used-car prices also eased for a third straight month as dealer inventories recovered. Food prices were roughly flat, while energy costs edged lower after a drop in gasoline.

Stripping out food and energy, the core measure that policymakers watch closely also came in below expectations. Services prices outside of housing remained firmer than goods prices, Sample Wire reported, a sign that the last stretch of the slowdown may be uneven.

The report strengthens the case for the Federal Reserve to continue lowering interest rates at its coming meetings. Cheaper borrowing would eventually show up in mortgage, auto and credit card rates, though analysts cautioned that the central bank will want to see several more months of cooling before committing to a faster pace.

Investors will look next to the jobs report and to the minutes of the Fed's last meeting for clues on timing. Any rebound in rents or a jump in wages could complicate the picture, Sample Wire said, but for now the trend is moving in the direction that households and businesses have been hoping for.

A ceasefire between Northland and Southmark largely held through its first full day, with international monitors reporting only minor violations along the Vell Valley line, Example Times reported on Friday. Observers described the incidents as isolated exchanges of small-arms fire that did not escalate.

The monitoring team said it had deployed to eight positions along the line and had recorded no use of heavy weapons since the truce took effect. Both governments said they remained committed to the agreement, though each accused the other of testing it, according to Example Times.

Residents in border villages who had sheltered for weeks began returning to check on their homes, and aid convoys were cleared to move along two roads that had been closed. Relief agencies said the most urgent needs are clean water, medicine and fuel for heating as temperatures drop.
Energy markets also reacted. Concerns about disruption to regional pipelines and shipping had pushed prices higher during the fighting, and traders said a durable pause would help steady them.

The next several days are seen as critical. Negotiators are expected to meet to discuss a longer-term arrangement, including the withdrawal of forces from the valley and a mechanism for resolving disputes. Example Times noted that earlier truces in the conflict collapsed within a week, so monitors will watch closely for any buildup of troops near the line.

Halcyon, a fictional rocket startup, successfully landed a booster on an ocean barge on its third attempt, the company said, according to Demo Daily. The first stage touched down upright after launching a batch of satellites into orbit, and recovery crews secured it hours later.

The two earlier tries ended badly. The first booster tipped over after landing, and the second ran low on fuel for its final burn and was lost at sea. Company engineers told Demo Daily that changes to the landing legs and the guidance software addressed both problems.

Halcyon said it plans to inspect the recovered booster and fly it again within months if the check goes well. Reuse is the key to lowering launch costs, since the first stage is the most expensive part of the vehicle. The company has said it hopes to cut the price of a launch by about a third once reuse becomes routine.

The milestone adds to competition in a crowded market. A small number of established providers dominate launches for commercial satellites and government payloads, and newcomers have struggled to match their reliability and price.

Analysts quoted by Demo Daily said one landing does not prove a business, and that Halcyon still needs to show it can recover boosters repeatedly and on a tight schedule. The company's next launch is scheduled for later this year, and customers will be watching whether it can repeat the feat.

A House committee voted 30 to 19 on Thursday to advance legislation that would set national safety rules for the largest artificial intelligence models, Sample Wire reported. The bill now heads to the full House, where its prospects are less certain.

Under the measure, developers of the biggest systems would have to test them for dangerous capabilities before release and report serious incidents to a federal agency. Smaller models and research projects would face lighter requirements, according to Sample Wire.

The House Commerce Committee vote was not strictly along party lines. Several members of both parties said they supported a federal standard, while others objected to the cost of compliance and to what they described as vague definitions of which models would be covered. Amendments narrowing the testing requirements were adopted before the final vote.

If it becomes law, the bill would be the first federal statute governing AI. It would also override a growing patchwork of state rules, a feature that technology companies have sought and that some state officials have opposed, arguing that states should be free to set stricter limits.

The Senate has not yet taken up a companion bill, and House leaders have not said when they will schedule a floor vote. Sample Wire noted that the legislative calendar is crowded, so supporters will need to move quickly if they hope to pass the bill before the end of the session.

Automakers are racing to secure supplies of high-strength magnets after China imposed new export limits, with two fictional carmakers warning that production could slow if licenses take more than a month to arrive, Example Times reported.

The magnets, which contain rare earth elements, are used in electric motors, power steering and other components. China produces most of the world's supply, and the China Commerce Ministry has said the new licensing requirement is meant to protect national security and will not ban shipments outright.

One of the carmakers told Example Times it holds roughly six weeks of magnet inventory and has asked suppliers to apply for licenses early. The other said it is looking at redesigning some motors to use less of the material, but that such changes would take a year or more.

The restrictions follow earlier steps by Beijing to limit exports of critical minerals, a move that has already unsettled supply chains for electronics and clean energy equipment. Industry groups have urged governments to speed up efforts to build processing capacity outside China, although new mines and refineries take years to come online.

Shortages would hit electric and hybrid models hardest, since they use more magnets per vehicle, and could push up prices for buyers. Analysts will be watching how quickly the ministry approves applications over the next few weeks, Example Times said, because delays beyond a month would begin to affect factory schedules.

GreenBot, a fictional maker of robotic lawnmowers, announced a recall of about 300,000 units on Thursday after discovering that a sensor fault could allow the blades to keep spinning when the mower is lifted, Demo Daily reported.

The company said the lift sensor is meant to cut power to the blades immediately if the machine is picked up or tipped. In affected units, the sensor can fail to register the movement, creating a risk of cuts to hands or feet. GreenBot said it has received a small number of reports of minor injuries and no reports of serious harm.

The recall covers several models sold over the past three years through home improvement stores and online retailers. Owners can find the model and serial number on a label under the mower's body, and the company has posted a lookup tool on its website, according to Demo Daily.

Customers are advised to stop using the mowers until they are repaired. GreenBot said it will provide a free fix, either a replacement sensor kit that owners can install themselves or a prepaid shipping label for a repair at a service center. The company said it expects to begin shipping the kits within two weeks.
Consumer safety officials said they are reviewing the recall, and Demo Daily noted that owners who bought a mower secondhand may need to register it to receive the repair.

Treasury yields fell sharply on Friday as traders raised their bets that the Federal Reserve will cut interest rates faster than previously expected, Sample Wire reported. The yield on the benchmark 10-year note dropped to its lowest level since spring.

The move followed a report showing that consumer inflation cooled to 2.6% last month, below forecasts. Bond prices, which move in the opposite direction of yields, rose across the curve, with shorter-dated notes that are more sensitive to Fed policy seeing some of the largest gains.

Futures markets now put higher odds on back-to-back rate cuts at the central bank's next two meetings, according to Sample Wire. Several strategists said the inflation data removed a major worry that the slowdown in price growth might stall.

Falling yields matter for ordinary borrowers because mortgage rates tend to follow the 10-year note. Lenders often adjust their quotes within days, so buyers and homeowners thinking about refinancing could see lower rates in the coming week, though the pace of any decline will depend on whether yields hold their drop.

Not everyone is convinced the rally will last. Some analysts warned that strong jobs data or a pickup in wages could quickly reverse the trend, and that heavy government borrowing continues to put upward pressure on yields. Traders will watch next week's economic releases and speeches from Fed officials for further direction.

Smoke from wildfires blanketed three western states on Friday, triggering air quality alerts that covered about 20 million people, Example Times reported. Fires burned across dry hillsides and forest land, fanned by strong winds.

Health officials in the affected areas urged residents to stay indoors where possible, keep windows closed and run air purifiers. Schools in several communities moved recess inside or canceled outdoor sports, and some airports reported hazy conditions that slowed arrivals, according to Example Times.

Fire crews said more than a dozen large fires were active, with the biggest threatening foothill neighborhoods. Evacuation orders were issued for thousands of residents, and emergency shelters opened in nearby towns. Firefighters said low humidity and gusts made it difficult to build containment lines, and forecasters do not expect meaningful rain for several days.

Doctors say fine particles in smoke can aggravate asthma, heart disease and other conditions. Children, older adults, pregnant women and people with lung problems are most at risk, and officials recommend well-fitted N95-style masks for anyone who must go outside. Filters in home heating and cooling systems should be checked and replaced if clogged.

Scientists have noted that smoke seasons are growing longer as drought and heat extend the fire season. Example Times said the alerts could last through the weekend, depending on how winds shift and whether crews gain ground against the largest fires.

Workers at the Port of Calloway ratified a three-year contract that includes a 9% wage increase, ending a strike that had snarled cargo traffic in the region, Demo Daily reported. Ships began unloading within hours of the vote.

Union members approved the deal by a wide margin after negotiators reached a tentative agreement earlier this week. In addition to the raise, the contract includes improvements to overtime pay and limits on automation of certain crane operations, according to Demo Daily. Port management said it was pleased the work stoppage was over.

Dozens of container vessels had been waiting offshore, and trucking companies reported long delays for pickups. Shipping lines had begun rerouting some cargo to other ports, adding costs that retailers warned could be passed on to shoppers.

Logistics experts told Demo Daily that clearing the backlog will take time. Cranes and crews will work extended shifts, but congested yards and a shortage of trucks and chassis will limit how fast containers can move out. They estimated that normal operations could resume in two to three weeks.

That timeline matters for retailers who depend on the port for holiday merchandise, and many are hoping goods will arrive in stores before the peak shopping weeks. Industry groups said they will watch for any further delays, and noted that the three-year deal should give the port some labor stability going forward.

Qubitron, a fictional quantum computing company, said it has reached a milestone in error correction, demonstrating logical qubits that preserved data ten times longer than the physical qubits they were built from, according to Sample Wire.

Quantum bits are extremely fragile, and noise from heat, vibration and stray electromagnetic fields causes them to lose information quickly. Error correction spreads one logical qubit across many physical ones so that mistakes can be detected and fixed. The challenge has been getting the corrected qubit to perform better than its parts, a threshold that Qubitron says it has now crossed on its latest processor.

The company shared its results in a technical paper and said they were achieved over repeated runs rather than in a single best case. Independent researchers have not yet reviewed the claims, Sample Wire noted, and several outside experts said they would want to see the full data and how the result holds up as systems get larger.

Error correction is widely seen as the main hurdle before quantum computers can tackle useful problems such as designing new materials or breaking certain kinds of encryption. Current machines are too error-prone to run long calculations, and scaling up will require many thousands of reliable logical qubits.
Qubitron said its next goal is to link multiple logical qubits and run simple algorithms on them. Sample Wire reported that the company plans to open the system to outside researchers next year.

Teachers in the fictional Ridgeport school district went on strike on Friday, closing schools for tens of thousands of students after contract talks over class sizes and pay collapsed overnight, Example Times reported.

Union leaders said negotiators had worked until after midnight but could not close the gap with the district on staffing limits for crowded classrooms and a raise that would keep pace with the cost of living. District officials said they had offered a pay increase but that the union's full demands would exceed what the budget can support, according to Example Times.

Picket lines formed outside dozens of schools early in the morning. The district said buildings will stay closed while the strike continues, and it has opened a handful of sites to provide meals for students who rely on free lunches. Many parents scrambled to arrange child care, and some employers allowed staff to work from home.

The walkout is the third major teacher strike in a big city this year, as districts struggle with tight budgets after federal pandemic aid ran out and enrollment declined. Union leaders across the country have pointed to rising housing costs and teacher shortages as reasons for demanding higher pay.
Both sides said they are willing to return to the table, and a state mediator has offered to help. Example Times reported that talks could resume as early as this weekend, but no date has been set.
The US Navy unveiled a prototype of an autonomous submarine on Friday, showing a 50-foot uncrewed vessel that it says can patrol for months without surfacing, Demo Daily reported.

Navy officials said the craft runs on a battery system and a quiet propulsion unit, and uses onboard software to navigate and avoid obstacles without a human at the controls. It is designed to carry sensors for monitoring ships and other submarines, and could later be fitted with other payloads, according to Demo Daily.

The prototype will begin sea trials in the coming months, the Navy said, with tests focused on endurance, reliability and the ability to communicate with commanders when needed. Officials declined to say how many vessels they hope to build or what each would cost, but described the program as a low-cost complement to crewed submarines rather than a replacement.

Defense analysts say uncrewed undersea vehicles could change how the United States monitors contested waters, especially in the Pacific, where the Navy is looking for ways to widen its coverage without stretching its fleet. Several other nations are developing similar craft.

Questions remain about how well autonomous boats can handle the harsh and unpredictable ocean, and how they would be protected from interference. Demo Daily noted that Congress has asked the Navy for regular updates on the program's progress and its budget.

African Union leaders endorsed a plan to create a continental payments system that would let businesses settle cross-border trade in local currencies, Sample Wire reported. The decision came at a summit of member states on Friday.

Under the fictional system described in the plan, a trader in one country could pay a supplier in another without first converting funds into dollars or euros. Payments would clear through a shared platform linked to national banks. Officials said the aim is to cut fees and shorten settlement times, which can run to several days today.

Supporters argue that the change would lower costs for small and medium-sized companies, which often struggle with the expense of moving money across borders. Intra-African trade remains a small share of the continent's total commerce, and leaders have repeatedly cited payments as one of the obstacles, according to Sample Wire.

Details still have to be worked out. Member states must agree on who will govern the platform, how it will handle exchange rate swings, and what safeguards will be in place against fraud and money laundering. Some central banks voiced concerns about losing control over monetary policy and about the technology needed to join.

A technical committee has been asked to deliver a detailed proposal in the coming months, and Sample Wire said a pilot involving a small group of countries could begin next year if the work stays on track.
Huddle, a fictional chat app, said on Friday that a misconfigured server exposed the email addresses and phone numbers of about 4 million users for roughly a week, Demo Daily reported.

The company said an internal storage server was left open to the internet after a routine update, and that a security researcher alerted it to the problem. Huddle closed access within hours of the report, according to Demo Daily. It said the exposed data did not include passwords, message contents or payment details, and that it has found no evidence so far that the information was misused.

Even so, security experts warn that contact information can be valuable to criminals. Email addresses and phone numbers can be used to send convincing phishing messages or to attempt to take over accounts through password resets. Users are advised to be suspicious of unexpected texts and emails that claim to come from Huddle or ask them to click a link.

Huddle said it is notifying affected users and has hired an outside firm to review its systems. It recommended that people change their passwords, turn on two-step verification and avoid reusing passwords on other sites.

Regulators in several countries may look into whether the company followed data protection rules, and Demo Daily noted that such laws can carry large fines for exposures of this size. The company has not said whether it expects to face penalties.
Japan and South Korea signed an agreement on Friday to secure their chip supply chains, pooling stockpiles of key materials and sharing alerts about possible shortages, Sample Wire reported.

Under the deal, the two governments will coordinate reserves of materials used in semiconductor manufacturing, such as specialty gases and chemicals, and let companies in either country draw on them in an emergency. They will also set up a channel to share early warnings about disruptions, from natural disasters to export restrictions, according to Sample Wire.

The pact reflects growing concern about the vulnerability of chip supply. Both countries are central to the industry, with South Korea home to major memory and processor makers and Japan supplying much of the equipment and materials that factories need. Relations between the neighbors have warmed in recent years after a long dispute over trade controls.

Officials said the arrangement is not aimed at any single country, though analysts noted that it comes as China tightens export limits on some critical minerals and the United States pushes allies to coordinate on technology policy.

US companies rely on parts and chips from both nations, so any disruption would be felt in American factories, from cars to consumer electronics. The two governments said working groups will meet within weeks to settle details, and Sample Wire reported that other partners could be invited to join the arrangement later.

Power grid operators in Texas warned that electricity supplies could be tight this winter, particularly during long cold snaps, according to a fictional reliability report cited by Example Times. The report was prepared with input from ERCOT, which runs the state's main grid.

It found that demand could outstrip available generation during extended periods of extreme cold, especially if gas plants have trouble getting fuel or if other plants go offline unexpectedly. Solar output is also lower in winter and wind can be unreliable, the report noted, leaving the grid dependent on thermal power in the early morning and evening hours.

A major factor is the rapid growth of electricity demand from data centers, which are being built in the state faster than new power plants and transmission lines can be added. Industrial customers and population growth are adding to the load, according to Example Times.

ERCOT said it has taken steps to prepare, including requiring more power plants to be winterized, adding backup reserves and improving coordination with gas suppliers. Officials stressed that the outlook does not mean blackouts are expected, but that the risk rises if a severe storm hits.

Residents are likely to be asked to conserve power at peak times if conditions tighten. Example Times said lawmakers and regulators are expected to review proposals this winter to speed up construction of new generation and to require large new customers to bring their own power or reduce usage in emergencies.
A federal appeals court on Friday blocked a new rule that would have expanded overtime pay eligibility, ruling that the agency overstepped its authority under labor law, Demo Daily reported.

The rule would have raised the salary level below which salaried employees must be paid time and a half for hours beyond 40 a week. The Labor Department estimated that about 4 million workers would gain overtime protection. Business groups and several states sued, arguing that the department had no power to set the threshold so high and had ignored the effect on small employers.

In its decision, a panel of the court agreed that the agency had gone beyond what Congress allowed, according to Demo Daily. The judges did not rule on whether the policy itself was wise, saying only that the law did not give the department the authority to issue it in that form.

For now, the existing salary threshold stays in place, and workers who were expecting to qualify for overtime will not. Employers that had begun adjusting pay or schedules in anticipation of the rule may have to reverse course or decide whether to keep the changes voluntarily.

Worker advocates criticized the ruling and said the administration should appeal. The Labor Department said it is reviewing the decision and weighing its options, which could include asking the full court to reconsider or taking the case to the Supreme Court. Demo Daily noted that such an appeal could take many months.

Researchers at Meridian AI, a fictional lab, said they have trained a robotics foundation model that learns to perform tasks by watching online video, using about 100,000 hours of footage, according to Sample Wire.

The team said the model watched videos of people cooking, cleaning and handling tools, and learned to predict how actions lead to results. It was then adapted to control a robot arm using a small amount of robot-specific data. In tests, the robot completed tasks such as opening drawers and loading a dishwasher, though its success rate varied and fell on unfamiliar objects, Sample Wire reported.

Collecting demonstrations on real robots is slow and costly, since each one requires a human operator and hardware time. Video, by contrast, is abundant. If machines can learn broad skills from it, developers could build more general-purpose robots without gathering vast data sets of their own.

Outside experts cautioned that translating what a person does on screen into precise robot movement is difficult. Differences in body shape, camera angle and lighting can trip up a system, and videos rarely show forces or touch. Results from a single lab also need to be reproduced.

Meridian AI said it plans to publish its methods and release a smaller version of the model for other researchers. Sample Wire reported that the company intends to test the system on more complex, multistep tasks, and in real homes and workplaces, over the coming year.
